opus-5.5.text:
I think there are real advantages on both sides, and it's worth being honest about that.

Large incumbents obviously have a lot going for them: huge amounts of capital, compute, existing hardware and manufacturing expertise, and in some cases big deployed fleets that could, in principle, generate a lot of data. If you're a company that already builds cars or warehouses or consumer devices, you have distribution and supply chains that a startup just doesn't have on day one.

But I think startups have a few advantages that are underrated right now. The first is focus. Robotics, especially the kind of general-purpose robot learning we're excited about, needs a team that's all in on that problem. In a large company, robotics is often one bet among many, and it can get deprioritized or pulled toward whatever the core business needs. At a startup, the whole organization is oriented around making robots actually work in the real world.

The second is speed and willingness to take a different technical bet. A lot of the progress we've seen recently comes from rethinking the approach: training on diverse data across many robot platforms, leaning on vision-language models, building foundation models for physical intelligence instead of narrow, task-specific systems. Incumbents often have legacy pipelines and existing products they need to protect, which makes it harder to throw things out and start from a cleaner foundation.

Third, talent. Many of the researchers who are most excited about this space want to work somewhere where the research and the product are tightly coupled and where they can have outsized impact. Startups can offer that.

And finally, the field is still early. We don't yet have the equivalent of a mature, scaled product where incumbents' distribution advantages dominate. The bottleneck right now is really the core capability — getting robots to generalize and be reliable — and that's a problem where a small, very focused team can make a lot of progress. Once the technology is more mature, the dynamics might shift, and things like manufacturing and deployment at scale will matter more. But at this stage, I think the advantage tilts toward teams that can move fast and stay focused on the fundamental problem.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting question, and I think the honest answer is that it's a bit of a mixed picture. There are things the big companies have that are hard to replicate, and there are things that startups have that are really hard for incumbents to pull off.

So on the incumbent side, the obvious advantages are compute and capital. A lot of the progress we're seeing in robot learning right now is coming from scaling, both in terms of data and in terms of model size, and that requires resources. If you're a startup, you're not going to have ten thousand GPUs lying around, and you're also probably not going to be able to deploy a fleet of robots at the scale that a large company can. And then there's distribution. If you already have a product that people use, you have a channel to get robots into the world, whether that's warehouses or consumer devices or whatever it is.

But I think the advantages on the startup side are actually really significant, and maybe underappreciated. The first is focus. Robotics is a problem where the details really matter. The hardware, the data collection process, the way you handle failures in deployment, how you think about the evaluation, all of that has to be tightly coupled. In a big company, those pieces often live in different orgs with different incentives, and it's very hard to iterate quickly across the whole stack. A startup can have the hardware team, the learning team, and the deployment team sitting next to each other and make a decision in an afternoon that might take a quarter somewhere else.

The second thing is that the field is still early enough that we don't actually know what the right recipe is. In language, by the time most startups were getting into it, the basic approach was fairly clear and the question was mostly execution and scale. In robotics, there are still real open questions. What's the right data mix? How much do you rely on teleoperation versus simulation versus autonomous data collection? What does the right action representation look like? How do you get robust behavior out of these models in the real world? When the recipe is still uncertain, being small and willing to take a bet on a particular approach is actually an advantage, because you can commit to a direction and find out quickly whether it works. Big companies tend to be more conservative, and they tend to hedge across many approaches, which slows everything down.

The third thing I'd point to is talent and culture. A lot of the people who really understand how to make these systems work are people who have spent years being frustrated by robots not doing what they want, and they're attracted to environments where they can actually ship something. I think startups are often able to attract people who want ownership and who want to see the loop close between research and the real world.

And then I'd say the last piece is that the data moat in robotics is not something incumbents automatically have. In language, the big companies had the internet. In robotics, nobody really has a huge, high quality dataset of robots doing things in the world. That has to be built, and it has to be built on purpose. So in some sense everyone is starting closer to the same line than you might expect, and the question becomes who can collect the right data most efficiently and who can learn from it most effectively. That's a place where a well run startup can genuinely compete.

So I guess if I had to summarize, I'd say the incumbents have an edge in raw resources and in distribution, but the startups have an edge in speed, focus, and in being able to make real bets while the field is still figuring out what works. And I think we're at a moment where the second set of advantages matters a lot, maybe more than it will in a few years once things are more settled.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest advantage startups have is focus. Robotics is a really broad space, and it’s easy to build a compelling demo without building something that’s useful. A startup can pick a particular customer need and get very tight feedback between deploying the robot, seeing where it fails, collecting data, and improving the system.

The large companies have real advantages in compute, talent, and the ability to invest over a long time horizon. Hardware is expensive, so those resources matter. But a small team can often move faster and make decisions across the whole stack—hardware, software, data collection—without having to coordinate across a lot of different organizations.

So I don’t think it’s necessarily a question of who has the best model at a particular moment. It’s also who can build the fastest learning loop in the real world. And that’s a place where a startup can be very competitive.

sol-6.1.text:
I think startups have an advantage in focus and speed. You can pick a particular application, build the hardware and software around it, and iterate closely with customers. In robotics, that feedback loop matters a lot, because things that look good in a lab don’t necessarily work reliably in the real world.

Large companies have advantages in capital, infrastructure, and the ability to invest over a long time horizon. But a startup can make deployment its central priority and organize the whole company around getting a system to work. A lot depends on whether that deployment gives you a useful learning loop: you put robots out there, understand where they fail, and use that experience to improve the next version.
